chapter_title: Setting Up Your First Cucumber Project

screens.title: Set Up Your First Cucumber Project
screens.subtitle: From a minimal Maven project to a passing Gherkin scenario

narration.text: In this lesson we will set up a minimal Behavior-Driven Development project using Cucumber for Java. You will learn the conventions for where to place feature files and step definitions, how to declare the core dependencies in a build file, how Gherkin steps map to Java methods, and how to configure a test runner so Cucumber executes your scenarios. We use Maven in the examples to keep the workflow reproducible, and we build a simple calculator scenario to show the full loop from specification to assertion. This setup matters because it turns human-readable requirements into automated checks, making feedback fast and reducing manual regression work. By the end, you will be able to create a feature, implement steps that capture arguments like integers, run tests with mvn test, and diagnose common setup problems such as missing glue paths or incompatible dependency versions. Think of this as the scaffolding that makes future BDD work reliable and repeatable.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: A simple project structure plus the right dependencies and runner settings lets Cucumber map Gherkin to Java and run scenarios automatically.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives show the concrete skills you will gain while setting up a Cucumber project. First, you will learn how to create a standard project layout that keeps human-readable specifications separate from test code. That matters because the build tool expects feature files in resources and step classes in test code, which simplifies test discovery. Second, you will add dependencies to the build file so Cucumber and JUnit are available during test scope. Proper dependency management avoids runtime errors and ensures compatible APIs. Third, you will author a simple Gherkin feature that describes a behavior in plain language. Writing clear scenarios increases communication with non-technical stakeholders. Fourth, you will implement step definitions that accept placeholders such as integers, capture state, and use assertions to verify outcomes. This implements the link between specification and executable checks. Each objective includes a short competency milestone to confirm you've set up and run a passing scenario in your project.

screens.title: Project Structure Conventions
screens.subtitle: Where to place features, step definitions, and runners

narration.text: A consistent project structure makes test discovery predictable. For Java projects using Maven or Gradle, place feature files under src/test/resources and Java classes such as step definitions and test runners under src/test/java. This convention keeps human-readable specifications separate from executable code. Feature files in resources are discovered by the Cucumber runner, while step classes in the test java package resolve the glue. A concrete example: create src/test/resources/features/calculator. feature and implement steps in src/test/java/com/cohortia/steps/CalculatorSteps. java. If you stray from this layout, you risk Cucumber not finding your scenarios or JUnit not compiling your tests. One common misconception is that feature files can live under src/main; putting them there mixes test specifications with production artifacts and can complicate packaging. Key takeaway: follow the convention so your build tool and Cucumber can find files without extra configuration. Now, check that your IDE marks the resources folder as test resources so the compiled test classpath includes your feature files. Project Structure Conventions means feature files in src/test/resources and test code in src/test/java keep discovery and packaging simple.. In practical terms, where to place features, step definitions, and runners. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

  • Correct placement prevents "Undefined steps" due to unreachable glue paths.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Add Cucumber and JUnit Dependencies
screens.subtitle: Minimal pom.xml for a test-scoped Cucumber setup

narration.text: Dependencies are declared in the build file. For Maven, the pom. xml lists cucumber-java, cucumber-junit, and junit under test scope so they are available during testing but not bundled in production artifacts. Declaring the Java compiler source and target ensures compatibility with your JDK. The provided minimal pom includes properties for cucumber and junit versions. A common misconception is to add Cucumber to compile scope. That bloats the main artifact and risks shipping test libraries. Here the dependencies are test scoped, which is the right choice for executable specifications. When adding versions, prefer using properties so you can update them in one place. If you rely on Gradle instead, the same dependencies are added via testImplementation in your build. gradle. Always check compatibility between Cucumber and JUnit versions to avoid runtime errors. Add Cucumber and JUnit Dependencies means use test scope for cucumber and junit to keep test libraries out of production artifacts..   <artifactId>bdd-first-project</artifactId>
  <version>1.0-SNAPSHOT</version>

    <cucumber.version>7.14.0</cucumber.version>

  </properties>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.cucumber</groupId>
      <artifactId>cucumber-java</artifactId>
      <version>${cucumber.version}</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.cucumber</groupId>
      <artifactId>cucumber-junit</artifactId>
      <version>${cucumber.version}</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>junit</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit</artifactId>
      <version>${junit.version}</version>

    </dependency>

  • If you use Gradle, add equivalent test dependencies using testImplementation or testCompileOnly.
Key Takeaway

Declare Cucumber and JUnit as test-scope dependencies and manage versions with properties to avoid compatibility issues.

screens.title: Write a Gherkin Feature
screens.subtitle: A plain-language scenario to specify behavior

narration.text: Gherkin provides a readable syntax to describe behavior. A feature groups scenarios that explain user-facing behaviors, and each scenario uses Given, When, Then to define preconditions, actions, and expected outcomes. For example, a basic calculator feature can describe adding two numbers. Writing clear steps matters because they become the specification that developers and testers implement. Place your feature at src/test/resources/features/calculator. feature. A common misconception is to place implementation details inside the Gherkin; avoid this by keeping steps focused on behavior, not how the UI works. The example on this slide shows a minimal scenario for adding two positive numbers. Use placeholders like integers to keep steps reusable. Keeping features concise helps teams read specifications quickly and map them to step definitions without ambiguity.   I want to perform basic arithmetic operations

screens.title: Implement Step Definitions
screens.subtitle: Map Given/When/Then to Java methods with placeholders

narration.text: Step definitions bridge the readable Gherkin steps to executable code. In Java, annotate methods with @Given, @When, and @Then. Use Cucumber expressions like {int} to capture numeric values from steps and receive them as method parameters. The example CalculatorSteps class maintains a numbers list and computes a result. Inside the Given method, integers are added to state. The When method performs an operation such as addition, and Then asserts the expected result using JUnit's Assert. assertEquals. A useful tip is to keep state minimal and reset it at the end of the scenario so tests remain independent. A common misconception is that annotations must contain exact text; instead use placeholders to create reusable step definitions. This approach keeps feature files readable while allowing flexible, testable implementations. Implement Step Definitions means use @given/@when/@then and cucumber expressions like {int} to capture values and implement behavior in java.. In practical terms, map given/when/then to java methods with placeholders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Step mapping
keyIdea.text: Use @Given/@When/@Then and Cucumber expressions like {int} to capture values and implement behavior in Java.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Implement Step Definitions
CalculatorSteps.java
package com.cohortia.steps;

import io.cucumber.java.en.Given;
import io.cucumber.java.en.When;
import io.cucumber.java.en.Then;
import org.junit.Assert;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class CalculatorSteps {
  private List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
  private int result;

  @Given("I have entered {int} into the calculator")
  public void i_have_entered_number_into_the_calculator(int number) {
    numbers.add(number);
  }

  @When("I press the add button")
  public void i_press_the_add_button() {
    result = numbers.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).sum();
  }

  @Then("the result should be {int} on the screen")
  public void the_result_should_be_result_on_the_screen(int expectedResult) {
    Assert.assertEquals(expectedResult, result);
    numbers.clear();
  }
}
Explanation
  • Annotations map Gherkin steps to methods. Placeholders like {int} parse values automatically.
  • Maintain small state for scenario execution and clear it at the end to avoid leakage.
  • Use assertions from your test framework to verify expected outcomes.
Misconception: exact-text matching is unnecessary when you use Cucumber expressions and placeholders; they make steps reusable.

screens.title: Configure the Cucumber Test Runner
screens.subtitle: Using @RunWith and @CucumberOptions to point to features and glue

narration.text: A TestRunner class tells JUnit to use Cucumber as the test engine and where to find features and step definitions. Use @RunWith(Cucumber. class) and @CucumberOptions to configure features, glue, and reporting plugins. The features option points to the path where your Gherkin files live, and glue specifies the package where Cucumber should scan for step definitions. Forgetting the glue option or pointing it to the wrong package is the most frequent cause of undefined steps. The plugin option can include human-readable console output and an H T M L report. Running the runner executes all scenarios found under the features path. Keep the glue paths aligned with your package structure, for example com. cohortia. steps, so Cucumber resolves annotations correctly. This configuration is simple but crucial: it is the bridge between static feature files and executable code. Configure the Cucumber Test Runner means set features and glue in @cucumberoptions so cucumber links feature files to step classes during test execution.. In practical terms, using @runwith and @cucumberoptions to point to features and glue. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Runner configuration
keyIdea.text: Set features and glue in @CucumberOptions so Cucumber links feature files to step classes during test execution.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Configure Test Runner
TestRunner.java
package com.cohortia.runners;

import io.cucumber.junit.Cucumber;
import io.cucumber.junit.CucumberOptions;
import org.junit.runner.RunWith;

@RunWith(Cucumber.class)
@CucumberOptions(
  features = "src/test/resources/features",
  glue = "com.cohortia.steps",
  plugin = {"pretty", "html:target/cucumber-reports.html"}
)
public class TestRunner {
}
Key settings
  • features: path to Gherkin files. Use test resources paths.
  • glue: package(s) where step definitions live; must match your Java package names.
  • plugin: reporting options like pretty console output and HTML reports.
Common mistake: wrong glue package causes "Undefined steps" even when your step classes exist.

screens.title: Run Your Tests with Maven
screens.subtitle: Build, execute scenarios, and read the report

narration.text: Running your Cucumber scenarios is a simple sequence. From the project root, run mvn test. Maven will compile test classes, resolve test-scoped dependencies, and run the TestRunner which in turn executes Cucumber. You should see console output indicating scenario execution and a plugin-generated H T M L report under target/cucumber-reports. html. If tests fail, the console shows stack traces and the H T M L report provides a scenario-level view. A common point of confusion is thinking mvn test runs only unit tests; it runs any tests bound to the test lifecycle, including the Cucumber runner. If dependencies fail to download, check your Maven settings and internet access. If steps are undefined, verify feature paths and glue settings. The report file gives a clear pass/fail summary you can share with teammates for faster feedback. New step method
@When("I press the subtract button")
public void i_press_the_subtract_button() {
  if (numbers.size() < 2) {
    throw new IllegalStateException("Not enough numbers to subtract.");
  }
  result = numbers.get(0);
  for (int i = 1; i < numbers.size(); i++) {
    result -= numbers.get(i);
  }
}

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Remedies
screens.subtitle: Undefined steps, wrong glue, and version mismatches

narration.text: When a project fails to execute scenarios, three issues appear frequently. First, undefined steps occur when Cucumber cannot match Gherkin to step definitions. The usual cause is an incorrect glue path in @CucumberOptions. Verify the package name matches where your step classes live. Second, putting feature files in the wrong directory prevents discovery; ensure they are under src/test/resources and that your features path in the runner points there. Third, dependency version mismatches between Cucumber and JUnit can cause class or runtime errors. Use the chapter's minimal pom approach and keep versions in properties for easier updates. A useful debugging sequence is: check the features path, confirm glue packages, run mvn -X for verbose output, and inspect the H T M L report for failing scenarios. These steps quickly narrow the root cause and get your suite passing. Common Pitfalls and Remedies means check glue, feature locations, and dependency versions in that order to resolve most setup issues.. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Common Pitfalls
Problem: Undefined steps
Cause: glue path mismatch or step classes in an unexpected package. Remedy: ensure @CucumberOptions glue points to the package containing your step definitions, e.g., com.cohortia.steps.
Problem: Missing features
Cause: feature files not under src/test/resources or wrong features path in the runner. Remedy: move features to resources and set features = "src/test/resources/features".
Problem: Version incompatibility
Cause: mismatched Cucumber and JUnit versions. Remedy: manage versions in properties and consult compatible version pairs before upgrading.
Quick debug sequence
  1. Confirm features path and file locations.
  2. Check glue package names and runner configuration.
  3. Verify dependency versions and run with verbose logs.
